name: Question 13
problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{y(y-1)}{x}=0,\,y(-1)=2,\,x<0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation*

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}-\frac{1}{x}z=-\frac{1}{x}
$$

*using the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{-1}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}-\frac{z}{x}=-\frac{1}{x}\,.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-\frac{1}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|x{|}^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{|x|} \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x<0.$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=-\frac{1}{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}z) & =-\frac{1}{x}\cdot (-\frac{1}{x}) \\ -\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}z & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}z) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}z)\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{x}z & =\frac{1}{x}+C \\ z & =1+Cx.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =1+Cx \\ y & =\frac{1}{1+Cx}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now determine $C$ from the initial condition $y(-1)=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{1}{1-C}\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{(1+\frac{1}{2}x)} \\  & =\frac{2}{2+x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Solve the initial value problem dydx−y(y−1)x=0,y(−1)=2,x<0. Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation dzdx−1xz=−1x using the substitution z=y−1.

a
y=x1+ex
b
y=22+x
c
y=41−x
d
y=−exx+2
e
y=3−x1−x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The substitution z=y−1 transforms the given equation into the equation dzdx−zx=−1x.

The above equation is in the standard form dzdx+P(x)z=Q(x) with P(x)=−1x,Q(x)=−1x. We then compute an integrating factor: I(x)=e∫P(x)dx=e−∫(1/x)dx=e−ln⁡|x|=eln⁡|x|−1=1|x|=−1x under the condition that x<0.

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by I(x)=−1x yields −1x⋅(dzdx−1xz)=−1x⋅(−1x)−1x⋅dzdx+1x2z=1x2ddx(1xz)=−1x2.

So, we have ∫ddx(1xz)dx=−∫1x2dx1xz=1x+Cz=1+Cx.

Next, we determine y(x) by writing z=y−1. This results in y−1=1+Cxy=11+Cx.

We now determine C from the initial condition y(−1)=2: 2=11−C⟹C=12

So, we have y=1(1+12x)=22+x.
